messages.subject: Random intercepts in a picture naming experiment
messages.subject_clean: Random intercepts in a picture naming experiment
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm analyzing data for picture naming experiment where we're looking at the
effects of Frequency and Phonological Neighborhood Density (PND) on
reaction times. I'm following Barr et al. (2013)'s recommendation and
trying to keep the random effects structure maximal. I'm including random
intercepts for subjects as well as by-subjects random slopes for the all
the predictors. However,  for pictures, because a given picture has only
one value for frequency/PND, by-picture random slopes do not make sense.

My questions is about including random *intercepts *for pictures. I
initially included them, but now I'm thinking a big part of why a picture
is hard/easy to name overall is because it's frequent/infrequent or because
it has a spare or dense PND. So, by including random intercepts for
pictures, I might be taking away variance that would have otherwise been
explained by the fixed effects? Am I increasing the probability of making a
Type II error, by including intercepts for pictures?

Thank you in advance for your help!

Hossein

messages.subject_clean: Random intercepts in a picture naming experiment
messages.body_plain:
Dear Hossein,

The magnitude of the picture intercepts should go down as your fixed
effects do a better job of capturing between-picture differences. But it’s
good to keep them to account for other factors that are not in your fixed
effects  (eg name agreement, picture complexity).

mg

messages.subject: Re: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.subject_clean: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Steve,

I'm not sure if anyone responded to this previously (apologies for
duplication if so).

   - You can certainly build the model with a random intercept for items
   and a fixed effect for group.
   - You cannot have a random slope for group, as not all items have
   observations at both levels of group.
   - This may be anticonservative, as you're failing to take in to account
   the dependencies between observations of items across different levels of
   group.

The various alternatives (analyzing only overlapping items, only distinct
items, or all items) all seem to have drawbacks, so I'm not entirely sure
what to recommend. One way to proceed would be to conduct all of the
analyses and show how the estimate for the group effect varies as a
function of which set of items is included. If it's similar across
analyses, that might increase your confidence in the effect.

mG

> items as a random effect in such a model? Is there any concern that the

messages.body_plain:
Hi ling-r-lang community,

I am looking for help in setting contrasts in R in a better way than I have
been able to do for variables with multiple levels.
One of my independent variables has a lot of levels (10). I would like to
compare the different levels to one of those, A. I used the "relevel"
option to try to do this, but I am not sure this did what I wanted as when
I look at my contrasts, I do not see any "-1", only 0s and 1s (see below).

              B      C        D       E        F       G       H      I
   J

Would there be a better solution to try to do this?
I have tried multiple things but have not had much success.

Thanks!

Stephanie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie,

You are using treatment coding, which (as you intended) compares reach
level against the reference level (the one that is zero for all contrasts;
in this case level "A"). So you are good to go.

Florian

messages.subject: Re: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.subject_clean: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Steve,

Florian Jaeger and I had an off-list conversation about this. Since the
random slope of group by items is estimating a distribution over items,
some of the items can be omitted and the model will still fit. In fact, it
actually has a reasonable good estimate for the item-specific effects of
group. Please see attached code for results.

In these data there are some convergence issues, but these seem to be
highly dependent on the particular items excluded (and the particular
distribution of participants across groups). This gets quite a bit worse as
the number of overlapping items gets smaller and smaller. A more systematic
study with simulated data is definitely in order, but I haven’t done that.

An alternative approach which won’t suffer from the same convergence issues
is to use a Bayesian model. That might be the right way to go in this case.

Thanks, Florian, for discussion of this!
Matt
